segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Good morning everyone.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Last week we were looking at the hunter-gatherers in Ireland, across the Irish Sea from England.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Today, we're going to move on to the period between four and six thousand years ago, known as the Neolithic period, which is when a total farming economy was introduced in Ireland.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now, there are several hypotheses about the origins of the first Neolithic settlers in Ireland, but most of these contain problems.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For instance, there are considerable archaeological difficulties about the theory that they came from England.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The evidence doesn't really add up.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But there are even greater practical problems about the theory that they came directly from continental Europe.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For one thing, it's not clear just how sufficient numbers of men and women could have been transported to Ireland to establish a viable population.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: As you know, the hunter-gatherer economy which existed beforehand was based on small scattered groups.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The farming economy would almost certainly have required much larger communities to do all the work needed to plant and tend sufficient crops to sustain them through the year.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The early farmers kept various animals, including cattle and sheep.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: There's also evidence of pigs, but it is possible that these could have been descended from the native wild species.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now, we know from modern farming that if the level of breeding stock falls below about three hundred females, the future of the species locally is at risk.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So we must assume that from the beginnings of Neolithic farming the number of breeding sheep would have considerably exceeded three hundred. and the national cattle herd must have been of a similar size.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The question is how these were brought to the area and where they came from.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It's usually suggested that the Neolithic settlers used skin-covered boats to transport livestock.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But this method would have severely restricted the range of the colonising fleets.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The sheer volume of animal transport necessary means it's unlikely that this livestock could have been brought from anywhere further than England.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: What about crops?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Well, two main cereal crops were introduced to Ireland during this time: wheat and barley, both in several varieties.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The main evidence for their presence consists of impressions on pottery. where a cereal grain accidentally became embedded in the surface of a pot before it was fired.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The grain itself was destroyed by the firing, but it left an impression on the pot which could be studied and identified by botanists.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Let's turn our attention now to the farming technology available at that time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Before the cereal crops could be planted, it would have been necessary to clear the forest and to break the ground by ploughing.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The stone blade of a plough has been discovered during excavation in County Mayo in western Ireland.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The body of the plough would have been of wood and could have been drawn by people, but it's also likely that cattle were used.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now, the cultivation of crops and the husbandry of livestock brought about changes in people's lifestyle such as the type of shelters they made.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For one thing, instead of moving from place to place they needed permanent dwellings.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The stone axes used to chop down trees to make these dwellings were far superior to any that the Stone Age hunter-gatherers used.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: To make the axes, sources of suitable stone had to be found and systematically exploited.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These so-called 'axe factories' were really quarries rather than factories, as the manufacture of the axes wasn't regularly performed on the quarry site.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: However, after the axe had been . chipi)ed into shape, they needed water and sand for grinding and polishing, so a high mountainside wouldn't have been an appropriate place for this.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So this final stage of the manufacture must have been carried out close to water and sure enough, there's ample evidence of this at coastal sites.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now it's clear that these Neolithic axes were transported all over Ireland, as well as to Scotland and the south of England.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It's not really surprising that axes from 'axe factories' in England have also been found in Ireland.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: At the very least, this indicates that there was a link between the two islands during that period.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: One of the most useful innovations of the colonisers was pottery making, which was quite unknown to Irish hunter-gatherers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The pottery was probably made by shaping clay into a ball with the hand, and then hollowing it until the walls were the right thickness.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: After firing, the outside was often polished.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This would have helped the pots to retain water, as they weren't glazed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now we know that the clay used usually came from lQQll sources, which suggests that manufacture was on a fairly small scale, even though thousands of fragments are usually found at Neolithic sites.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In the course of time decoration began to appear.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: At first this looked like a series of stitches and was just around the~ of the pots.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This could have been an imitation of earlier vessels which were made of leather sewn onto wood.

SECTION 4 Questions 31-40
Questions 31-34
Choose the correct letter, A, B or C
IRELAND IN THE NEOLITIDC PERIOD
Ireland
England
31 According to the speaker, it is not clear
A when the farming economy was introduced to Ireland.
B why people began to farm in Ireland.
C where the early Irish farmers came from.
32 What point does the speaker make about breeding animals in Neolithic Ireland?
A Their numbers must have been above a certain level.
B They were under threat from wild animals.
C Some species died out during this period.
33 · What does the speaker say about the transportation of animals?
A Livestock would have limited the distance the farmers could sail.
B Neolithic boats were too primitive to have been used.
C Probably only a few breeding animals were imported.
34 What is the main evidence for cereal crops in Neolithic Ireland?
A the remains of burnt grain in pots
B the marks left on pots by grains
C the patterns painted on the surface of pots
